node.title: Molecular Basis of Inheritance: Structure and packaging of DNA helix; Search for genetic

questions.stem: Which nitrogenous base is present in RNA but is absent from DNA?
questions.explanation: RNA contains the bases adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil, while DNA contains adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine. Uracil takes the place of thymine in RNA, and it pairs with adenine during transcription.

optionRationale.2: Thymine is found in DNA, and RNA has uracil in its place.
optionRationale.3: Adenine is present in both DNA and RNA.
optionRationale.4: Guanine is present in both DNA and RNA.

questions.objective: Identify the base specific to RNA

questions.stem: In eukaryotes the nucleosome is formed when about 200 base pairs of DNA are wrapped around
questions.explanation: Histones are positively charged basic proteins, and eight histone molecules form a unit called the histone octamer. The negatively charged DNA is wrapped around this octamer to form a nucleosome, the repeating unit of chromatin that looks like beads on a string.

optionRationale.1: The core is made of eight histone molecules, not four.
optionRationale.3: Non-histone proteins are involved in higher levels of packaging, but the nucleosome core is histone.
optionRationale.4: Ribosomal proteins belong to ribosomes and play no role in DNA packaging.

questions.objective: Describe the structure of a nucleosome

questions.stem: The enzyme that catalyses the synthesis of RNA on a DNA template is
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase is a DNA-dependent RNA polymerase. It binds to the promoter, reads the template strand and joins ribonucleotides, so a complementary RNA is formed in the 5' to 3' direction. This process is called transcription.

optionRationale.1: DNA polymerase makes DNA from a DNA template during replication.
optionRationale.2: Reverse transcriptase makes DNA from an RNA template, which is the reverse of transcription.
optionRationale.4: DNA ligase joins DNA fragments and does not synthesise RNA.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a stop (termination) codon?
questions.explanation: Of the 64 codons, three do not code for any amino acid. They are UAA, UAG and UGA, and they signal the end of translation. AUG is the start codon for methionine, UUU codes for phenylalanine and GGG codes for glycine.

optionRationale.1: AUG codes for methionine and acts as the start codon.
optionRationale.2: UUU codes for the amino acid phenylalanine.
optionRationale.3: GGG codes for the amino acid glycine.

questions.stem: Okazaki fragments are formed during DNA replication on the
questions.explanation: DNA polymerase can synthesise DNA only in the 5' to 3' direction. On the strand that runs the other way the DNA is made in short pieces, called Okazaki fragments, as the fork opens. This is the discontinuously synthesised lagging strand, and the fragments are joined later by DNA ligase.

optionRationale.1: The leading strand is made continuously, without fragments.
optionRationale.3: Only one of the two strands is made in fragments.
optionRationale.4: A primer is a short starter sequence; the fragments are pieces of the new DNA strand.

questions.objective: Identify the strand with Okazaki fragments

questions.stem: In Griffith's experiment with Streptococcus pneumoniae, the mice died when they were injected with
options: heat-killed R-strain and S-strain bacteria alone
live R-strain mixed with heat-killed S-strain bacteria
questions.explanation: Mice injected with live R strain, or with heat-killed S strain alone, lived. When live R bacteria were mixed with heat-killed S bacteria the mice died, and live S bacteria could be recovered. Some transforming principle from the dead S cells changed the R cells into virulent S cells.

optionRationale.1: Heat-killed S-strain bacteria are dead and cannot cause the disease on their own.
optionRationale.2: The R strain is non-virulent, so mice injected with it alone lived.
optionRationale.3: With no live bacteria present, the mixture could not cause disease.

questions.objective: Recall the result of Griffith's experiment

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about DNA replication.
A. DNA polymerases catalyse polymerisation only in the 5' to 3' direction.
B. The discontinuously made fragments are joined by DNA ligase.
C. Replication in E. coli starts at a specific origin of replication.
D. The leading strand is synthesised discontinuously.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: DNA polymerases work only in the 5' to 3' direction (A), the short fragments on the lagging strand are joined by DNA ligase (B), and replication begins at a specific origin of replication (C). The leading strand is made continuously, so statement D is wrong.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is also correct, so this is incomplete.
optionRationale.2: Statement A is also correct, so this is incomplete.
optionRationale.4: Statement D is false; it is the lagging strand that is made discontinuously.

questions.stem: Match List-I (RNA) with List-II (role) and choose the correct code.

right: I. Adapter that carries an amino acid to the ribosome
II. Precursor of mRNA in eukaryotes that undergoes splicing
III. Structural and catalytic component of the ribosome
IV. Carries the genetic message from the gene for protein synthesis

questions.explanation: mRNA carries the genetic message from the gene (A-IV). tRNA is the adapter that brings amino acids to the ribosome (B-I). rRNA is the structural and catalytic part of the ribosome (C-III), and hnRNA is the primary transcript of eukaryotes that is spliced to give mRNA (D-II).

optionRationale.2: A and B are interchanged; the adapter is tRNA and the message is carried by mRNA.
optionRationale.3: C and D are interchanged; hnRNA is the precursor of mRNA, not the ribosomal component.
optionRationale.4: A and C are interchanged; mRNA does not form the ribosome.

questions.objective: Match types of RNA with their roles

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The genetic code is nearly universal.
Reason (R): AUG codes for methionine and also acts as the initiation codon.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: The same codon codes for the same amino acid in almost all organisms from bacteria to humans, so the code is nearly universal. AUG does code for methionine and also serves as the initiation codon. But this is a separate property of the code and does not explain its universality.

optionRationale.1: The dual role of AUG describes one codon and does not explain why the code is shared by almost all organisms.
optionRationale.3: R is true; AUG is both the methionine codon and the start codon.
optionRationale.4: A is true; the genetic code is universal with few exceptions.

questions.objective: Distinguish properties of the genetic code

questions.stem: In a double-stranded DNA molecule 22 per cent of the bases are guanine. The percentage of adenine is
questions.explanation: By Chargaff's rule, guanine pairs with cytosine, so cytosine is also 22 per cent and G + C is 44 per cent. The remaining 100 - 44 = 56 per cent is A + T. Since adenine equals thymine, adenine is 56 / 2 = 28 per cent.

optionRationale.1: 22 per cent is the value for guanine and cytosine, not adenine.
optionRationale.2: 56 per cent is the sum of adenine and thymine together.
optionRationale.4: 44 per cent is the sum of guanine and cytosine together.

questions.stem: The distance between two adjacent base pairs in DNA is 0.34 nm. The length of a DNA molecule of $6.6 \times 10^{9}$ base pairs is about
questions.explanation: The length is the number of base pairs times the distance between them: $6.6 \times 10^{9} \times 0.34 \times 10^{-9}$ m, which is $6.6 \times 0.34 = 2.24$ m, so about 2.2 m. This is the length of the DNA in a diploid human cell, which fits into a nucleus only because of tight packaging.

optionRationale.1: 0.22 m is ten times too small and comes from a decimal slip.
optionRationale.2: 22 m is ten times too large and comes from a decimal slip.
optionRationale.3: 1.1 m is the length for the haploid number of base pairs, about half of the given number.

questions.objective: Calculate the length of DNA from base pairs

questions.stem: In the lac operon of E. coli, the genes z, y and a code respectively for
questions.explanation: The gene z codes for beta-galactosidase, which breaks lactose into galactose and glucose. The gene y codes for permease, which increases the permeability of the cell to lactose, and the gene a codes for transacetylase. All three are expressed when the operon is switched on by lactose.

optionRationale.2: z and y are interchanged; z codes for the hydrolysing enzyme, not for permease.
optionRationale.3: The order is reversed; a codes for transacetylase, not for beta-galactosidase.
optionRationale.4: y and a are interchanged; permease is coded by y.

questions.objective: Recall the products of the lac operon genes

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the Human Genome Project.
A. It was a 13-year project launched in 1990 and completed in 2003.
B. The average gene size is about 3000 bases.
C. Less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins.
D. The functions of all the genes discovered were known by the end of the project.
Which statements are correct?
questions.explanation: The project began in 1990 and was completed in 2003, so A is correct. The average gene is about 3000 bases long, so B is correct, and less than 2 per cent of the genome codes for proteins, so C is correct. The function of over 50 per cent of the discovered genes was unknown, so D is wrong.

optionRationale.1: Statement C is also correct, so this misses it.
optionRationale.3: Statement D is false, and statement A is left out.
optionRationale.4: Statement D is false, and statement B is left out.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements on the Human Genome Project

questions.stem: An mRNA reads 5'-AUG CCG UAA-3'. The number of amino acids in the polypeptide formed from it is
questions.explanation: Translation starts at AUG, which codes for methionine, and the next codon CCG codes for proline. The third codon UAA is a stop codon and codes for no amino acid, so it only ends translation. The polypeptide therefore has two amino acids, not three.

optionRationale.1: This counts the stop codon as an amino acid, but UAA only terminates translation.
optionRationale.2: This counts only the start codon and misses the codon CCG, which codes for proline.
optionRationale.4: There are only three codons, so four amino acids is impossible.

questions.objective: Count amino acids from an mRNA with a stop codon

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): In bacteria, translation can begin before transcription of the mRNA is complete.
Reason (R): Bacterial mRNA needs no processing, and there is no nuclear membrane separating transcription from translation.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: In bacteria the mRNA is active as soon as it is made, with no splicing, capping or tailing, and the nucleoid is not enclosed by a nuclear membrane. Ribosomes can therefore attach to the growing mRNA, and translation begins before transcription finishes. In eukaryotes the nucleus separates the two processes.

optionRationale.2: R directly explains A, since processing and compartment separation are what would otherwise delay translation.
optionRationale.3: R is true; bacterial mRNA is not processed and there is no nucleus.
optionRationale.4: A is true; coupled transcription and translation occurs in bacteria.

questions.objective: Explain coupling of transcription and translation in bacteria
